lede: A bar chart shows how many by how tall. When the groups are different widths that breaks down: a narrow group and a wide one can hold the same number and look nothing alike. A histogram fixes it by letting the area of each bar, not its height, carry the count.
can: Work out a frequency density for every class before drawing.
Draw the bars touching, with both axes labelled.
Read a frequency back as the area of a bar.

md: On an ordinary bar chart the height of a bar is the count, which works only while every bar is the same width. Widen one group and its bar towers over the others for no honest reason. A histogram makes the **area** of each bar the count instead, so the height becomes a rate and the eye compares areas.

caption: Frequencies 8, 24, 15, 10, 3 over widths 10, 15, 10, 20, 20. The tallest bar is the second, even though the third class holds fewer values per bar of width; the widest classes are the lowest.

md: The height of a bar is therefore a rate: values per unit of the variable, called **frequency density**. So frequency density $=$ frequency $\div$ class width, and everything in this topic — drawing the bars, reading them back, estimating the median — comes from area of bar $=$ frequency.

prompt: A class $0 < t \le 10$ has frequency 20. What is its frequency density?
explain: Frequency ÷ class width: 20 ÷ 10 = 2. The width is 10, not 0 or 20.

title: Why area and not height
md: A bar's area is height $\times$ width. If the height is values per unit, multiplying by the width in units gives values — the frequency itself. That is why the area of every bar reads as a count, whatever width the class happens to be.

title: Not on the formula sheet
md:
$\text{frequency density} = \dfrac{\text{frequency}}{\text{class width}}$ and so $\text{frequency} = \text{frequency density} \times \text{class width}$.

Neither line is on the page-2 formula sheet. They were printed on the temporary extended sheet used in Summer 2022 and Summer 2023 only; since 2024 the Higher sheet carries no statistics formulae at all, so these are recall.

prompt: A bar for $5 < x \le 8$ has frequency density 4. What is its frequency?
explain: Frequency = density × width = 4 × 3 = 12. The bar's area, not its height, is the count.

prompt: A 12-mark histogram question on M4: roughly how long should it take?
explain: M4 is 100 marks in 120 minutes, about 1.2 minutes a mark, so 12 marks is about 14 minutes.

md:
The Summer 2025 paper gave a table and an empty grid. The routine is fixed:

1. Write the **width** of every class.
2. Add a **frequency density** row: frequency ÷ width, every class, before drawing anything.
3. Choose the vertical scale from the **largest density**, not the largest frequency, so the tallest bar uses most of the grid and the smallest bar is still visible. Check the last class fits horizontally.
4. **Label** both axes: Frequency density; the variable with its unit.
5. Draw the bars between their exact boundaries, **touching**.

The marks follow the same order: the density row, then scales and labels, then the bars.

prompt: Which label goes on the vertical axis of this histogram?
explain: The heights are densities. In Summer 2025 the label was part of a separate mark; a correct picture with the axis labelled Frequency lost it.

md: Frequency is area, so for any bar: frequency $=$ height $\times$ width. For **part** of a class, assume the values are spread evenly and take that fraction of the width. If the class $25 < l \le 40$ holds 18 values, then the values above 30 are $\dfrac{10}{15} \times 18 = 12$. A count above some value starts from the right-hand bars: add whole bars until the next one would take you past the count, then take the fraction you still need from that bar. Always check the total: if you rebuild every frequency and they do not add to the number in the stem, a boundary or a width has been misread.

prompt: The bar for $20 < x \le 30$ has height 1.5. What is its frequency?
explain: Height × width = 1.5 × 10 = 15. The height alone (1.5) is the density, not the frequency.

md:
The median is the middle **value**, so it splits the **area** in half, not the axis.

1. Position: $n \div 2$.
2. Add the frequencies class by class (cumulative frequency) until you reach the class that contains that position.
3. Values still needed $=$ $n \div 2$ minus the cumulative frequency before that class.
4. Median $\approx$ lower boundary $+ \dfrac{\text{needed}}{\text{class frequency}} \times \text{class width}$.

Step 2 earns the first mark and is where most candidates stop, series after series. Step 4 is the discriminator: the midpoint of the class, or the middle of the axis, earns nothing further.

prompt: 30 values, cumulative frequencies 3, 12, 24, 30. The class $10 < j \le 20$ holds 12 values. Estimate the median.
explain: Position 15; 12 done before the class, so 3 of the 12 are needed: 10 + 3/12 × 10 = 12.5. The midpoint 15 is not the median.

text: When the axis has no numbers

md: November 2025 printed a density axis with no scale and gave one bar's frequency instead. Calibrate from that bar: its density is frequency ÷ width; divide by its height in squares to find what one square is worth on the axis. Equivalently, divide the frequency by the bar's **area** in squares to find the frequency per square, then read every other bar by counting squares of area. Either route works; most successful candidates used the area-per-square version. Without this step nothing later in the question can start.

prompt: A bar for $30 < x \le 40$ is 6 large squares tall and represents 30 values. What is one large square worth on the vertical axis?
explain: Density 30 ÷ 10 = 3, over 6 squares: 3 ÷ 6 = 0.5. Dividing 30 by 6 ignores the width.

md: The histogram must become a table first: boundaries, widths, frequency $=$ density $\times$ width for every bar, and a check that the total matches. Then midpoints, $\sum fx$, and divide by $\sum f$ (the total frequency, never the number of classes). Keep the answer to one or two decimal places; a whole-number rounding loses the final mark. Check it sits inside the data and near the visual balance point of the picture.

prompt: You are asked for the mean from a histogram. What do you write first?
options: The bar heights, to add and divide by the number of bars
A table with widths and frequency = density × width for every bar
answer: A table with widths and frequency = density × width for every bar
explain: Heights are densities, and dividing by the number of bars is not a mean. The table comes first; n ÷ 2 starts the median, not the mean.

md: The last part almost always reuses the frequencies you have just found. Three things are marked:

prompt: In Summer 2025 the histogram question was Q22 of 22. Where should you expect it?
options: Near the start of the paper
Among the last two or three questions
It is not examined in M4
answer: Among the last two or three questions
explain: Every series since Summer 2023 has placed it at Q21 to Q23. Leave time for it.

md:
1. The **population** for the sample, which may be a sub-group (for example, only the patients who waited more than 6 hours), and the **group** inside it, often needing part of a class.
2. The share: group $\div$ population $\times$ sample size. Stopping at the group count, or at a percentage, is the most common zero.
3. A **whole number** of people, with one sentence of reasoning: "the sample keeps the same proportion as the population, so...". Where the exact value is halfway, the scheme accepts either neighbour.

prompt: 160 customers, 45 of them in one group. How many of a stratified sample of 32 come from that group?
explain: 45 ÷ 160 × 32 = 9 exactly. 45 is the group in the population, not in the sample.

md: A compare mark needs one sentence that uses **both** figures and says what the difference means in context: "the median this year is 26 mph, lower than last year's 29 mph, so vehicles were typically slower". A number on its own, or a comment about one year only, does not earn it. If asked whether a target has been met, write the two numbers being compared and the inequality between them before the word yes or no.

prompt: This year's median is 26 mph; last year's was 29 mph. Which sentence earns the compare mark?
options: Speeds were lower this year: median 26 mph against 29 mph last year
answer: Speeds were lower this year: median 26 mph against 29 mph last year
explain: Both values and a direction, tied to the context. The other two give one value or no value.

title: Chief Examiner, Summer 2025, Unit M4
md: Question 22 asked for a histogram on a blank grid, then an estimate of the median, then a stratified sample. A lot of candidates scored zero on the drawing because they did not find frequency densities first; those who did usually reached full marks, though some lost the scale-and-labels mark. On the median, most gained one mark for the class and did not know what to do next. The sampling part separated the most able; many left it blank.

prompt: In Summer 2025, what did the candidates who reached full marks on the drawing do first?
options: Chose a scale reaching the largest frequency
Drew the bars and labelled afterwards
explain: The report ties full marks to finding the densities first; the scale then comes from the largest density and the labels are a separate mark.

md:
Turn a frequency table into frequency densities and draw the bars.
Read a frequency back from a bar, or from part of one.
Estimate the median by splitting the area in half.
Rebuild a table from a histogram to estimate the mean.
Scale an unnumbered axis from one bar you are told about.

One of the last three questions, six to fourteen marks over three to five parts that feed each other. The first mark is the frequency density row. Stuck: take the parts in order and write the density column before anything else.

title: Not on this specification
md:
- Frequency polygons: the phrase does not appear anywhere in the CCEA specification, so no bar-tops-joined polygon is ever asked for
- Open-ended classes such as 60 < t: every CCEA class has two boundaries, so every bar has a width
- Frequency density on the formula sheet: it was printed only on the temporary extended sheet of Summer 2022 and Summer 2023; the page-2 Higher sheet since 2024 has no statistics formulae
- Histograms with equal widths and a Frequency axis are M1 bar-chart work (M1-HD strand), not this statement
